title: Byrd v. Lamar
lead: A student spent years waiting for specialized courses advertised by his university and allegedly promised by administrators. Circumstantial evidence allowed promissory-fraud claims against two officials to proceed, while distinct claims against other officials lacked proof or preservation.

actors.name: William Harris and Jacqueline Williams
actors.role: University president and student-affairs vice president

actors.name: Justice Lyons
actors.role: Author of the unanimous Alabama opinion

proceedings: University, contract, and official-capacity claims were dismissed on immunity grounds and not appealed. The Supreme Court partly reversed later individual-capacity summary judgments, remanding only promissory fraud against Lamar and Steptoe.
limits: The surviving claims presented jury questions, not established deception or damages. Defendants’ lack of testimony did not relieve Byrd’s burden. A reported attempt to arrange other education was evidence, not an enforced settlement.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The catalogue attracted a transfer student to music media
sections.cue: Introduce the program and initial delays.
paragraphs: Bernard Byrd transferred from Miami-Dade Community College to Alabama State University in fall 1995 for music media. Its catalogue promised recording, music physics, digital-signal processing, film and video production, an internship, and an advanced laboratory. Music dean Horace Lamar became his adviser and repeatedly required completion of core courses first, although the catalogue allowed prospective majors to start music in their first semester. Byrd took general music but no music-media courses during his first three years.

According to Byrd, Lamar said in 1997 and 1998 that an instructor was being sought. In February 1999, instructor Carol Porter reported Lamar’s admission that he was deceiving Byrd and another student. Lamar responded with assurance that a revised sequence still permitted May 2000 graduation. A spring recording instructor arrived weeks late and offered grades without completed work. These were summary-judgment accounts, not findings after trial.

sections.title: More promises produced schedules without adequate instruction
sections.cue: Trace the later evidence of knowledge.
paragraphs: After Byrd complained, academic-affairs vice president Roosevelt Steptoe apologized and promised courses soon. Lamar’s May 4, 1999 memorandum scheduled courses through summer 2000. Byrd enrolled in two fall courses but testified an instructor arrived about five weeks late, admitted inadequate qualifications, and displayed obsolete or broken equipment. Byrd rejected passing grades in exchange for minor computer work. Other professors reportedly said the program had ended before his enrollment and qualified instructors were unavailable.

By spring 2000 he chose to withdraw without a degree. Student-affairs vice president Jacqueline Williams referred him to Steptoe. Byrd said Steptoe then admitted the program did not exist and offered educational and living assistance, including tuition elsewhere, if Byrd dropped his lawyer. Byrd refused, seeking actual instruction and an end to misleading students. The alleged exchange supported arguments about earlier knowledge; it was not a settlement the court enforced.

sections.title: Only individual officials’ fraud claims remained on appeal
sections.cue: Separate immunity dismissals and summary-judgment burdens.
paragraphs: The original suit alleged contract and fraud against the university, officials, and trustees in official and individual capacities. The trial court dismissed the university, contract claim, and official-capacity claims under Alabama constitutional immunity. The amended complaint alleged ordinary fraud against Lamar and president William Harris, promissory fraud against Lamar and Steptoe, and suppression against Harris and Williams, naming trustees without a substantive claim. Later summary judgment disposed of individual claims.

Byrd did not challenge the university or official-capacity rulings and conceded judgment for trustees. The appeal concerned four officials individually. Depositions, affidavits, correspondence, schedules, academic records, and catalogues supplied evidence; defendants supplied no testimony, but Byrd still had to meet his burden. After a movant’s prima facie showing, substantial evidence had to permit fair-minded people reasonably to infer a disputed fact, viewed favorably to Byrd.

sections.title: The separately pleaded ordinary-fraud claims failed
sections.cue: Explain preservation for Lamar and missing attribution for Harris.
paragraphs: Lamar’s separately labeled ordinary-fraud claim actually concerned failure to disclose inaccurate catalogue information. Byrd argued misrepresentation in his opening appellate brief and accepted suppression only in reply. The court would not entertain a new reply theory or a complaint version absent below, so it affirmed that claim while separately considering future promises.

Harris invoked university immunity, but fraudulent individual conduct fell within the relevant exception, allowing merits review without reviving the university claims. Existing-fact fraud required material misrepresentation, reasonable reliance, and resulting injury. Catalogue inaccuracies alone did not connect Harris personally to preparing courses, knowing the descriptions, approving publication, or misleading Byrd. Presidency was not enough. Byrd showed no response to his complaint letter. Harris therefore retained summary judgment.

sections.title: Lamar’s repeated promises carried evidence beyond nonperformance
sections.cue: Explain why the future-promise theory survived.
paragraphs: Promissory fraud required the ordinary elements plus intent when promising not to perform and to deceive. Failure alone was insufficient, and recklessness did not replace intention, but subsequent events could illuminate earlier intent.

Lamar faced repeated assurances and delays, the reported Porter admission, schedules without qualified teachers or equipment, faculty accounts of discontinuance and absent recruitment, and another student’s corroborating affidavit. Together these created a jury question. The core-course argument did not establish that a real program existed but Byrd was ineligible: a referenced document was missing from the appellate record, and no evidence showed available specialized classes taken by others or refused by Byrd. The promise concerned genuine career instruction, not merely obtaining grades or a timely degree.

A hearsay objection came too late because defendants themselves submitted Byrd’s deposition without the relevant objection below. That preservation ruling did not make every reported faculty statement inherently admissible for all purposes.

sections.title: Steptoe’s alleged knowledge also required credibility assessment
sections.cue: Contrast the surviving promise claim with suppression.
paragraphs: Byrd’s affidavit described Steptoe’s early-1999 promises of timely completion and forthcoming classes. Later testimony asserted prior knowledge of the program’s absence and described the eventual admission and educational offer. Counsel had not challenged or developed the prior-knowledge testimony, and Steptoe submitted the deposition himself. The court treated it as factual evidence rather than mere speculation or recklessness; together with his academic role and specific promises it supported an inference of intent. Denial of prior knowledge created a jury dispute.

Suppression against Harris and Williams, however, required duty, actual knowledge and concealment, induced action or inaction, and harm. Knowledge of missing courses, unqualified teachers, or inadequate equipment was not established, nor was concealment even assuming knowledge. Williams’s only conversation occurred after Byrd decided to leave, and Harris’s receipt of the letter was unproved. Those judgments stood.

sections.title: The remand was limited to two promissory-fraud claims
sections.cue: Give the exact result and participation.
paragraphs: On September 27, 2002, the court affirmed judgments for Harris, Williams, and the trustees and Lamar’s ordinary-fraud judgment. It reversed only individual-capacity promissory-fraud judgments for Lamar and Steptoe and remanded, without damages, contract enforcement, or a final finding of fraud.
Justice Lyons wrote, with Chief Justice Moore and Justices Houston, See, Brown, Johnstone, Harwood, Woodall, and Stuart concurring. The decision was unanimous and contained no separate opinion.
